notes:
I've written notes for all 12 verses. Three limits shaped them:

- **Searching was capped.** The tool allowed only a few searches, so nearly everything comes from Bible Hub, StudyLight, Blue Letter Bible, Enduring Word, bible.org, CCEL, Ligonier, Precept Austin and catholic.com.
- **Many sources aren't here.** I found nothing usable from the Methodist, Lutheran, Pentecostal or Orthodox sites, from bibleodyssey.org or the netbible.org notes, or from any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching.
- **Traditions are only named when the page names them.** StudyLight labels Gill "Baptist · Calvinism." For other writers I give the name only.

**v. 1**
- Guzik: Isaiah 24 described coming judgment, especially the Great Tribulation, and this is the song believers sing in the middle of it. "I will" shows praise is a decision, not just a feeling. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-25/
- Keil & Delitzsch: Isaiah puts two words from the same Hebrew root side by side for emphasis. What He has executed is the realization of His faithfulness, and the reality of His promises. They describe the prophet as choir leader for the church of the future. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/25-2.htm
- Matthew Henry: All the operations of providence are according to God's eternal counsels, and all will be carried out in their time. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_025.cfm

**v. 2: which city? (the readings really differ)**
- No particular city:
  - The Pulpit Commentary says no particular city is pointed at; the prophet has in mind every city that has been an enemy of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/25-2.htm
  - Coffman agrees and adds that Thebes, Babylon and Nineveh were all destroyed within about a century of Isaiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/25-2.html
- Many cities: Calvin thinks the singular stands for many cities reduced to heaps. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/25-2.html
- Babylon: Barnes takes it as Babylon, and lists other views (Samaria, Rome as the seat of antichrist, Jewish readings about Rome or Gog and Magog). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/25-2.htm
- Babylon or Nineveh standing for something bigger: Ellicott says the prophet probably meant one of them, but the city also stands for the world-power opposing God in every age. The Babylon of Isaiah becomes the type of the mystical Babylon of the Apocalypse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/25-2.htm
- Rome (Gill): he thinks it best to interpret it of the city of Rome, meaning all "antichristian" states. This is an older Protestant reading. Same URL.
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: Babylon, a type of the seat of Antichrist, destroyed in the last days. Same URL.
- A symbol of human society without God:
  - Guzik, quoting Clements, calls it a picture of organised human society, a "Vanity Fair." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-25/
  - Bible.org says it stands for every capital of every human society which has tried to make its own way and meet its own needs without God. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-25
- Cambridge Bible (a more critical reading): the description is too vague to identify the city, which depends on how the prophecy is dated. If written during or just after the Exile, Babylon is the natural choice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/25-2.htm

**v. 3**
- JFB: "the city of the terrible nations" means collectively for the cities of the surrounding nations, not Babylon. Jerome says Jewish interpreters saw this as the saints' song once all prophecy is fulfilled. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-25.html
- Guzik sees two results of God's judgment: His people glorify Him, and the unrighteous fear Him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-25/

**vv. 4–5**
- Guzik: God deserves praise because He gives strength to the poor and needy; He even silences "the song of the terrible ones." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-25/
- A Bible Hub study note says "the breath of the ruthless is like a storm" points to Assyrian threats. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/25.htm
- Ironside: God has always been a refuge and comfort to His people, even in trial and sorrow. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/isaiah-25.html

**v. 6: the feast (Protestant teachers differ on when and where)**
- Literal, future and on earth (Guzik): he links it to the Marriage Supper of the Lamb (Rev 19:9) and says this great feast takes place *on earth*, not in heaven. It is a victory banquet after the final battle. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/isaiah/isaiah-25.cfm
- The gospel age now (Gill): it means rather of the Gospel dispensation, which lies in the ministration of the word and ordinances, not the saints' final glory in heaven. He argues that fat, forbidden under the law, points to the Messiah's times. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/25-6.htm
- The church:
  - The Geneva Bible notes say Zion means the church, gathered from Jews and Gentiles under Christ. Same URL.
  - Calvin stresses the contrast: God once seemed to feed only the Jews, but now admits the Gentiles too. https://www.ccel.org/study/Isaiah_25:6-8
- The blessings of the gospel (Spurgeon, a Baptist):
  - The dishes are justification and adoption; the wines are peace, assurance and communion with Christ.
  - "All people" includes the Gentiles.
  - In the gospel banquet there is not a single dish brought by man.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/25-6.html
- Spiritual, not literal (Ironside): We certainly are not to take this sixth verse as referring to some literal feast; it means spiritual refreshment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/isaiah-25.html
- The Lord's Supper (Sibbes): In the Sacrament you have a Feast, a Feast of varieties not only bread, but wine. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/sibbes_richard/TGF/ch01.cfm
- The background:
  - Keil & Delitzsch: the image comes from the meals eaten with peace offerings, so the feast is spiritual. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/25-6.htm
  - Cambridge Bible: "wines on the lees" are wines left on their sediment to gain strength, then strained. Same URL.
  - Maclaren sees an echo of Sinai, where a feast followed the vision of God. Same URL.
- Catholic: a catholic.com article notes a Jewish belief in a banquet when the Messiah came, seen in Isaiah 25:1-9, and connects it to the Mass. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/the-mass-the-temple-and-loraine-boettner

**v. 7: the shroud or veil**
- Ignorance of God:
  - Benson calls it a veil of ignorance of God, and of the true religion, and sees here the conversion of the Gentiles. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/25-6.htm
  - Guzik says the veil keeps the nations from seeing and obeying God, and links it to 2 Cor 3:15–16. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-25/
- Death itself:
  - Coffman says the next verse explains the veil: it is death. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/25-8.html
  - Talmage likewise calls death a veil that blinds people. https://biblehub.com/sermons/isaiah/25-8.htm
- The Catholic Douay-Rheims renders it the face of the bond with which all people were tied, and the web. https://biblehub.com/catholic/isaiah/25-6.htm

**v. 8: death swallowed up**
- Most read it as Christ's victory over death, finished at the resurrection:
  - Gill (Baptist) says this is physical death, which Christ swallowed up by dying on the cross. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/25-8.html
  - Benson and Poole: the Messiah destroys death's power by His death (Heb 2:14). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/25-8.htm
  - Ligonier: death's defeat has been accomplished, even though we still await the last day. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/god-will-swallow-death-forever
  - Guzik: a resurrected body is not a revived corpse but a new order of life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-25/
- A minority view: Vitringa and Rosenmüller took "death" to mean the nation's wars and disasters. Barnes rejects this for literal death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/25-8.htm
- "Forever" or "in victory"? Barnes says the Hebrew word can mean either, and the sense is close to Paul's. The Cambridge Bible prefers "He hath abolished death for ever" and thinks Paul's "in victory" (1 Cor 15:54) comes from his familiarity with Aramaic. Same URL.
- Pulpit Commentary: apart from Hosea 13:14, this was the first announcement that death would end. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/25-8.htm
- The Greek Septuagint reads very differently: Death has prevailed and swallowed men up. Same URL.
- Disgrace removed: Cambridge says later Jews felt their national disasters as a religious disgrace. Guzik takes "rebuke" to mean God's correction, which will no longer be needed. Same URLs.

**v. 9**
- Guzik: we will say "this is our God" then because we say it now (Luke 12:8). It is "*His* salvation," not one we made. These things are partly true now and fully true "in that day." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-25/

**v. 10: "this mountain" and Moab**
- The hand on the mountain:
  - Guzik: after the Great Tribulation, Christ reigns from Jerusalem. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-25/
  - Pulpit: God's hand over the spiritual Zion, the church. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/25-10.htm
- Why Moab?
  - Ellicott: Moab's god Chemosh was set up against the Lord, so Moab came to stand for all His enemies. The Hebrew for "dunghill" may play on the Moabite town Madmenah. Same URL.
  - Matthew Henry: Moab stands for all the enemies of God's people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/25-10.html
  - Gill names the "antichristian powers," including "Turks and Papists." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/isaiah/25-10.html

**v. 11: who is the swimmer? (a real split)**
- God: Matthew Henry says God spreads His hands like a swimmer to work hard for His people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/25-10.html Guzik also has God reaching out to bring the proud low. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-25/
- Moab: Keil & Delitzsch say comparing God to a swimmer in a manure pit would be offensive. The swimmer is Moab itself, struggling in vain with the "skill" or tricks of its hands. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/25-10.htm The NET Bible translation agrees. https://www.blueletterbible.org/net/isa/25/1/

**v. 12**
- Keil & Delitzsch: verse 12 says plainly what verse 11 says in a picture. One possible reading of the Hebrew would point to Kir-Moab. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/25-10.htm
- Guzik: everyone who opposes Christ's rule is brought "to the ground, down to the dust." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-25/
